title: Expert outlines causes, symptoms and prevention of food poisoning
text:
Expert outlines causes, symptoms and prevention of food poisoning
J. C. Wright
An ongoing outbreak of cyclosporiasis has sickened thousands nationwide, prompting renewed attention to food safety habits, according to a July 22 statement from Penn State Health News. Dr. Poonam Bai, an infectious diseases physician at Penn State Health and assistant professor of medicine at Penn State College of Medicine, provided guidance on avoiding foodborne illnesses and managing symptoms.
Foodborne illnesses, also known as food poisoning, differ from typical gastrointestinal bugs but share similar symptoms and treatments. They can be caused by parasites, viruses or bacteria in food or by toxins released by these organisms. Leafy greens are among the most common sources of foodborne illness—including the current cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to contaminated shredded iceberg lettuce—while fatal cases are more often associated with contaminated meat and poultry when mishandled or undercooked.
Bai said there are two main categories of foodborne illness: those caused by toxins released by pathogens in the food—which produce nausea, vomiting and diarrhea within hours—and those caused by infections with viruses or bacteria such as Salmonella or E. coli or parasites like cyclospora. The latter can result in more severe symptoms including bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain that require immediate medical attention.
To reduce risk, Bai recommended good hand hygiene before handling foods along with proper cooking and refrigeration practices. "Make sure hot food stays hot and cold food stays cold," Bai said. She noted that contaminated foods do not necessarily look or smell bad: "It’s important to practice hand hygiene, cook your food properly and refrigerate it quickly because there is no way to tell just by looking at it." While washing fresh produce does not eliminate all contaminants, it can help reduce risk.
For most cases of mild illness, Bai advised rest, hydration with water or electrolyte drinks like Gatorade, eating bland foods such as crackers or bananas in small amounts, and monitoring for worsening symptoms. However, she said consumers should follow recall recommendations from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration if they suspect cyclospora infection after eating fresh produce: "Consumers should follow recall recommendations from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and seek medical attention if they develop persistent watery diarrhea, especially after eating fresh produce or restaurant salads." Symptoms may appear one to two weeks after exposure; diagnosis involves a stool test.
"Fortunately, once recognized, cyclospora is a treatable infection and early diagnosis helps reduce illness and prevent unnecessary complications," Bai said.
summary: Foodborne illnesses, also known as food poisoning, differ from typical gastrointestinal bugs but share similar symptoms and treatments. To reduce risk, Bai recommended good hand hygiene before handling foods along with proper cooking and refrigeration practices. For most cases of mild illness, Bai advised rest, hydration with water or electrolyte drinks like Gatorade, eating bland foods such as crackers or bananas in small amounts, and monitoring for worsening symptoms.
